title: More Memory, Worse Agents: Error Reproduction and Anti-Persistence in LLM Agents
content:
Computer Science > Artificial Intelligence
  [Submitted on 19 Oct 2026]
Title:More Memory, Worse Agents: Error Reproduction and Anti-Persistence in LLM Agents
View PDF HTML (experimental)
            Abstract:LLM agents can improve across tasks without updating model parameters by storing experience from their own executions in external memory and reusing it to guide later decisions. A central design question is whether to retain only observed trajectories and outcomes or also the rules, summaries, and skills inferred from them. Retaining these abstractions allows agents to reuse strategies without repeatedly deriving them from raw trajectories. However, errors in stored abstractions can propagate to subsequent decisions through retrieval and reuse. They can also shape execution trajectories, which then become the basis for new abstractions that reproduce the original errors. We term this feedback mechanism error reproduction: errors are regenerated through a cycle of abstraction, execution, and re-abstraction, extending their persistence beyond direct reuse of the original faulty knowledge. We propose Anti-Persistence, a memory design that accumulates trajectories and outcomes while reconstructing task-specific guidance on demand. An adaptive selector uses prior outcomes to decide whether and how to synthesize guidance, which is discarded after execution. This prevents its direct reuse as a stored object, although indirect feedback through retained trajectories remains possible. Across different benchmarks and backbones, Anti-Persistence achieves higher overall held-out success and the lowest average LLM-call cost among the evaluated memory designs. These results support separating experience accumulation from abstraction persistence in memorybased self-improvement.

report.summary: Storing inferred rules and skills in LLM agent memory can amplify errors; a new "Anti-Persistence" design keeps raw experience but discards abstractions after use.
report.background: Memory-based self-improvement has become a mainstream recipe for LLM agents: instead of retraining, an agent writes its own execution traces, outcomes, summaries or reusable skills into an external store, then retrieves them to guide later tasks. Frameworks like Reflexion (verbal self-reflection), Voyager (skill libraries) and MemGPT/Letta (tiered long-term memory) all assume that distilling experience into higher-level abstractions is strictly beneficial — it saves tokens and lets strategies transfer. The commercial memory layer (Mem0, Zep, LangMem and similar) is built on the same premise, selling 'learning' as a memory feature. What has been under-studied is the downside: once a wrong rule, bad summary or flawed skill enters the store, it is retrieved and reused, and it also steers the agent's actions, producing new traces that get re-abstracted into new rules carrying the same mistake. This October 2026 arXiv paper names that feedback loop and tests a memory architecture designed to break it.
key_points: Error reproduction is the core finding: a faulty abstraction is not just retrieved and reused once. It shapes the agent's execution trajectory, that trajectory is summarized into a new abstraction, and the original mistake is regenerated — persisting far beyond the lifespan of the bad memory that started it.

Anti-Persistence keeps only what was actually observed — trajectories and outcomes — and rebuilds task-specific guidance on demand. A fresh rule set is synthesized per task, used for execution, then thrown away, so it can never become a stored object that gets retrieved verbatim later.

An adaptive selector decides whether guidance is worth synthesizing at all, using the agent's prior outcomes as signal. This is also where the paper's cost win comes from: fewer stored abstractions means fewer retrieval and synthesis calls, and the design reports the lowest average LLM-call cost among the memory designs evaluated.

Across multiple benchmarks and backbones, Anti-Persistence delivers higher held-out success than the alternatives tested — that is, better performance on tasks the memory was not tuned on — directly contradicting the intuition that richer abstraction stores make stronger agents.

The authors are explicit about the residual risk: indirect error feedback through retained trajectories is still possible. Separating experience accumulation from abstraction persistence reduces but does not eliminate contamination, so memory hygiene remains an open engineering problem.
report.impact: For the AI industry, this challenges a selling point: "more memory, more skills, better agent" is not monotonic. Teams shipping memory layers will need to justify what they store, and vendors may need to offer ephemeral, per-task abstraction modes rather than ever-growing knowledge stores. For developers, the practical lesson is architectural — keep the raw log, generate guidance just-in-time, and treat persisted summaries and self-written skills as potentially toxic assets rather than free performance. It also argues for evaluating agents on held-out tasks, not on the tasks whose traces seeded the memory, since reuse-heavy designs can look strong in-sample while degrading. For regular users, this means agents that learn from their own mistakes may quietly compound them: expect fewer confident-but-wrong shortcuts, but also less of the pleasing "it remembers how I like things" behavior, and more re-derivation cost on repeated tasks.
report.tools: To follow up, look at memory frameworks you can swap architectures in: Letta (formerly MemGPT) for tiered agent memory, Mem0 and Zep for production memory stores, LangMem/LangGraph for configurable memory policies, and Cognee for graph-based memory. For the abstraction-as-skill side, compare with Reflexion and Voyager-style skill libraries, plus A-MEM for agentic memory notes. The paper's Anti-Persistence pattern is easy to prototype: store traces in a vector DB (Chroma, sqlite-vec) and add a per-task synthesis step with mandatory discard.
